extracted.intended_audience: academics and students in humor studies, linguistics, psychology, cognitive science, and related social sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying a formal, academically grounded theory of humor that explains when and why events or texts are perceived as funny, with attention to linguistic forms (puns, satire), social communicative functions, and physiological correlates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous Normality and Violation (N & V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs when a perceiver views a Situation simultaneously as being normal (N) and as constituting a violation (V) of the 'subjective moral order'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core necessary-and-sufficient condition of the theory: both interpretations must be available to the perceiver at once. Examples and logical analyses (e.g., puns) illustrate how a harmless-seeming 'normal' interpretation coexists with a 'violation' interpretation to produce humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective Moral Order
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'subjective moral order' is defined as the set of principles which an individual both has an affective commitment to and believes ought to hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What counts as a violation (V) depends on the perceiver's personal moral/affective commitments; variation among individuals and cultures in these commitments predicts variation in what they find funny. Use this to infer why people differ in responses to the same stimulus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-level scale of violations
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-level scale ranging from 'no violation' to 'funny violation' to 'threatening violation' depending on presence/absence or relative intensity of N and V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this scale to categorize responses: if V is absent, it's not funny; if V is present but mild and coexists with N, it is funny; if V is strong/threatening relative to N, the situation is threatening (not funny). This explains why some attempts at humor offend or fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: More-is-better principle for humor intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: The intensity of perceived humor is explained by a 'more is better' principle: greater (appropriate) presence or intensity of the relevant elements increases humor intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory uses a quantitative intuition: stronger, clearer, or more elaborated simultaneous N and V interpretations (without tipping into genuine threat) generally increase perceived funniness. This also informs judgments about escalation or understatement in joke-telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of presentation is irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The order in which N and V are presented in a joke or text is irrelevant to whether humor is perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor requires the simultaneous availability of the two interpretations, not a specific presentation order; thus rearranging the order shouldn't, in principle, change the core humor condition, though pragmatics may affect timing and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punning mechanism (linguistic ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns exploit linguistic ambiguity so that a violation in one interpretation is disguised by the 'straight' interpretation in the other; the pun depends on ambiguity between two meanings (e.g., 'a jar' vs 'ajar').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns of the set-joke/riddle type are often only mildly funny because (a) the logical inconsistency can be seen as a mild moral violation of discourse norms, and (b) once the listener resolves the ambiguity clearly the joke is simply wrong and the humor vanishes. The subtext of many puns is effectively 'go along with me; act stupid', which can provoke groans rather than belly laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire requirements (deadpan presentation & detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Written satire presents a Situation containing violations deadpan, without explicit acknowledgement; readers must detect the violation themselves for humor to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire often only persuades or is understood by readers who both detect the violation and already share the satire's evaluative stance. The deadpan stance can imply the existence of fooled or uncomprehending readers (whether or not they actually exist), increasing complexity of the humor. Empirical surveys show satire has persuasive impact mainly on those who already agree with its point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration as a generator of violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggerating an unremarkable personal quirk can transform it into a violation of norms (behavioral or appearance), thereby generating humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled exaggeration to push a trait into violating a norm while keeping a path to a normal interpretation available so both N and V coexist. This is a common mechanism in caricature and comedic amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule dynamics and moral status
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule imputes responsibility for a moral violation to a person or group and thereby damages their social status; targets who care about the laughers' opinions can be hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When humor functions as ridicule, it communicates a negative evaluative judgment (V) about the target. Consider ethical/social consequences: ridicule can be harmful and is not neutral comedy. Assess whether the audience shares the evaluative commitments that make ridicule effective or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embarrassment versus humor (temporal dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassment arises when a violator initially fails to understand a violation and then recognizes it; laughter may occur briefly during the moment of juxtaposition (N vs emergent V), but when full recognition (V) 'strikes home' the laughter stops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish early-stage laughter (confusion, nervousness, or a defensive tactic) from enduring humor. Laughter can also be used strategically to defuse embarrassment or signal lesser attachment to the violated principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tickling as physiological isomorphy (touch + pain = N + V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tickling involves simultaneous sensations of touch (normal) and pain (violation), mirroring the N and V elements of the theory and explaining properties like inability to tickle oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This physiological parallel supports the theory and suggests that both cognitive humor and ticklish laughter may share neural implementations. Use it as convergent evidence rather than as a production guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological similarity: laughter, crying, gasping
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter shares physiological features (repeated exhalatory vocalization) with crying and gasping in pain; laughter contains an element of emotional pain (the V interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This links affective components of humor to generalized pain responses and helps explain why laughter can be both pleasurable and contain an element of distress or aggression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of Inference for interpreting laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule: If a Situation lacks either N or V in one person's Interpretation, laughter by another implies that the other affective Interpretation is present in the laugher's mind and can be inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts (or participants) can use observed laughter to infer which interpretation (N or V) the laugher possesses. Conversely, suppression or feigned laughter signals deliberate communicative intent to avoid or convey an evaluative message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared humor requires shared affective evaluations (audience design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared humor requires a sharing of affective evaluations (values) among participants; effective joke-tellers must tailor material to their audience's moral viewpoints and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful humor demands more mutual understanding than mere passive listening. Comic performers must avoid evoking too-strong violations (which offend) or too-weak violations (which underwhelm). Use audience design principles to 'walk the emotional tight-rope'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression and feigned laughter as communicative tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoidance/suppression of laughter functions to avoid sending an inappropriate evaluative message; feigned laughter can be used to communicate an otherwise absent message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because people can produce laughter sounds without the internal experience, these behaviors should be interpreted contextually as intentional communicative acts rather than straightforward evidence of felt amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic application: infer others' moral attachments from laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand why others laugh (or don't), identify the principle being violated or the Interpretation under which the Situation seems normal; if someone laughs at a 'terrible' situation, infer they hold an Interpretation in which it is normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is a practical tool for probing others' moral commitments and emotional attachments. Note limitations: strong indignation may make people unwilling to seek or accept such explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and cognitive elaboration (explanation of repetition effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced humor on repetition is not necessarily due to lack of further cognitive elaboration; repeated exposure can remain funny if the violations and deadpan normality interpretations remain convincing (e.g., repeated successful Monty Python sketches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating why repetition reduces funniness, assess whether the N and V elements still co-occur convincingly and whether further elaboration matters for the audience. The theory disputes explanations that rest solely on loss of elaboration.
